title: will and shall 2
subtitle: will / won't for predictions; I shall / we shall
summary: Use will and won't to say what you know or believe about the future, not for things that are already arranged.

lesson.heading: Not will for arrangements
lesson.text: We do not use **will** to say what somebody has already arranged or decided to do. For that we use the present continuous or going to.

examples.text: **Are you going to watch** TV this evening?

lesson.heading: will = what we know or believe about the future
lesson.text: Kate has her driving test next week. Chris asks Joe: 'Do you think Kate **will pass**?' Joe answers: 'Yes, she's a good driver. **She'll pass** easily.' Joe believes that Kate will pass - he is *predicting* the future. When we predict a future happening or situation, we use **will / won't**.

examples.text: They've been away a long time. When they return, **they'll find** a lot of changes here.
'Where **will you be** this time next year?' '**I'll be** in Japan.'
That plate is hot. If you touch it, **you'll burn** yourself.
Anna looks completely different now. **You won't recognise** her.
When **will you get** your exam results?

left.label: is going to (decided)
examples: I think James **is going** to the party on Friday. (= I think he has already decided to go)

right.label: will (a prediction)
examples: I think James **will go** to the party on Friday. (= I think he will decide to go)

lesson.heading: We often use will ('ll) with these phrases
rows: Don't worry about the exam. I'm sure **you'll pass**.
Do you think Sarah **will like** the present we bought her?
I don't think the exam **will be** very difficult.
lesson.note: After I hope, we generally use the present: I hope Kate passes the driving test. I hope it doesn't rain tomorrow.

lesson.heading: will about now
lesson.text: Generally we use will to talk about the future, but sometimes we use **will** to talk about *now* - to say what we believe is true at this moment.

examples.text: Don't phone Amy now. **She'll be** busy. (= she'll be busy now)

lesson.heading: shall: only with I and we
lesson.text: Normally we use **shall** only with **I** and **we**. You can say I shall or I will (I'll), we shall or we will (we'll). In spoken English we normally use I'll and we'll. The negative of shall is **shall not** or **shan't**. We do not normally use shall with he/she/it/you/they.

examples.text: I **shall** be late this evening. (or I will be)
We **shall** probably go to France in June. (or We will probably go) - in speech: **We'll** probably go to France.
I **shan't** be here tomorrow. (or I won't be)

lesson.text: Ask whether the sentence reports a plan or a guess. A plan somebody has made is I'm doing / I'm going to; a guess, belief or prediction is will / won't.

exercises.prompt: I'm glad I'm meeting Emma tomorrow. It ___ be good to see her again.
exercises.explanation: A positive belief about the future: It'll be good.

exercises.prompt: Kate has her driving test next week. She's a good driver. ___ easily.
exercises.explanation: This is a prediction, not an arrangement, so we use will: She'll pass.

exercises.prompt: I've invited Anna to the party, but I don't think ___.
exercises.explanation: I don't think + will: I don't think she'll come.

exercises.prompt: The meeting is still going on. Ask when it is likely to finish, using do you think.
exercises.answer: When do you think it will end?
exercises.explanation: Question word + do you think + subject + will + verb.

exercises.statement: Lisa isn't free on Saturday. She'll work.
exercises.explanation: She's working. Something already arranged takes the present continuous, not will.

exercises.prompt: I've got some incredible news! You ___ believe it.
exercises.explanation: A negative prediction: You won't believe it.

exercises.prompt: Is the sentence about something already arranged or decided, or is it a prediction / belief?

items.text: Are you going to watch TV this evening?
I think James is going to the party on Friday.
I think James will go to the party on Friday.

exercises.prompt: I can't meet you this evening. A friend of mine ___ to see me.
exercises.explanation: The visit is already arranged, so the present continuous (is coming), not will.

exercises.prompt: The future situation is uncertain. Ask what is likely to happen, using do you think.
exercises.answer: What do you think will happen?
exercises.explanation: When the question word is the subject, will follows do you think directly: What do you think will happen?

exercises.statement: I hope Kate passes the driving test.
exercises.explanation: Correct. After I hope we generally use the present, not will.

exercises.prompt: *A:* Have you decided where to go for your holidays? *B:* Yes, ___ to Italy.
exercises.explanation: The decision has already been made, so we're going (not we'll go).

options: I shall be late this evening.
They shall probably go to France.
exercises.explanation: Shall is normally used only with I and we. With she or they use will.
